chunks: 15 — My father (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated to us, saying: Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Marrar narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to me from Yunus ibn Ya'qub.

He said: Abu 'Abdillah al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was with a group of his companions, among whom were Humran ibn A'yan, Mu'min al-Taq, Hisham ibn Salim, and al-Tayyar; and another group of his companions, among whom was Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who was a youth. Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: O Hisham! He said: At your service, O son of the Messenger of Allah. He said: Will you not inform me of what you did with 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and how you questioned him? Hisham said: May I be your ransom, O son of the Messenger of Allah! I hold you in great reverence and am abashed before you, and my tongue does not function in your presence. Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When I command you something, then do it. He (Hisham) said: News had reached me about 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd

and his sitting in the mosque of Basra, and that weighed heavily upon me. So I went out to him and entered Basra on a Friday. I came to the mosque of Basra, and there I found a large circle of people, with 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd wearing a black woollen cloak around his waist and another over his shoulders, while the people were posing questions to him. I asked the people to make way and they did. I then sat at the back of the gathering on my knees and said: O scholar, I am a stranger — will you grant me permission to ask you something? He said: Yes. I said to him: Do you have eyes? He said: O my son, what kind of question is this? I said: Such is my question. He said: O my son, ask, even if your question is foolish. I said: Answer me. He said: Ask. I said: Do you have eyes? He said: Yes.

I said: What do you see with them? He said: Colours and persons. I said: Do you have a nose? He said: Yes. I said: What do you do with it? He said: I smell scents with it. I said: Do you have a mouth? He said: Yes. I said: What do you do with it? He said: I distinguish the flavours of things with it. I said: Do you have a tongue? He said: Yes. I said: What do you do with it? He said: I speak with it. I said: Do you have ears? He said: Yes. I said: What do you do with them? He said: I hear sounds with them. I said: Do you have hands? He said: Yes. I said: What do you do with them? He said: I grasp with them. I said: Do you have a heart? He said: Yes. I said: What do you do with it? He said: With it I distinguish between all that reaches these limbs. I said: Are these limbs not sufficient without the heart?

He said: No. I said: How is that, when they are sound and healthy? He said: O my son, when the limbs are in doubt about something they have smelt, seen, tasted, heard, or touched, they refer it to the heart, which confirms certainty and dispels doubt. I said: So God has established the heart to resolve the doubts of the limbs? He said: Yes. I said: The heart is therefore indispensable; without it the limbs would not function correctly? He said: Yes. I said: O Abu Marwan, God — exalted be His mention — has not left your limbs without appointing a leader (imam) for them to confirm what is correct and resolve their doubt. Would He then leave all of creation in their perplexity, doubt, and disagreement without appointing an Imam to whom they may refer their doubts and confusions,

when He has given your own body an imam to whom you refer your perplexity and doubt?! He fell silent and said nothing. Then he turned to me and said: Are you Hisham? I said: No. He said: Have you sat with him? I said: No. He said: So where are you from? I said: From the people of Kufa. He said: Then you are he! Then he embraced me, seated me in his place, and did not speak until I arose. Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) laughed and said: O Hisham, who taught you this? I said: O son of the Messenger of Allah, it flowed upon my tongue. He said: O Hisham, this, by God, is written in the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa. (2).

key_terms.الإمام: Imam — the divinely appointed leader who resolves the doubts and perplexities of the community, analogous to the heart's role
key_terms.الجوارح: Bodily organs/limbs — the sensory faculties that perceive the external world but cannot resolve their own doubts
key_terms.الحيرة: Perplexity/bewilderment — the state of theological and moral confusion that afflicts humanity without an Imam
key_terms.الشك: Doubt — the uncertainty that the limbs/community cannot resolve on their own
key_terms.القلب: The heart — the organ of discernment that adjudicates the doubts of the limbs; used here as an analogy for the Imam
key_terms.صحف إبراهيم وموسى: The scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa — ancient divine scriptures attesting to the eternal truth of the Imamate

ai.seo_question: What is the hadith of Hisham ibn al-Hakam debating 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd about the necessity of the Imam?
ai.summary: This celebrated hadith from the Amali of al-Shaykh al-Saduq recounts how the young Hisham ibn al-Hakam, one of Imam al-Sadiq's most brilliant disciples, debated the Mu'tazilite theologian 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd at the mosque of Basra. Hisham used a masterful rational argument — drawing on the analogy of bodily organs needing the heart as a final arbiter of doubt — to establish that just as God does not leave the body without an authoritative organ to resolve its uncertainties, so too God cannot leave humanity without a divinely appointed Imam to resolve their theological and moral perplexities. The hadith culminates with Imam al-Sadiq authenticating the argument by declaring it is written in the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa, affirming both its divine origin and the theological principle of the necessity of the Imamate.
